newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. Commerce's Daley praises budget deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Commerce's Daley praises budget deal.

text.p: U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley revelled in the budget deal signed by President Clinton on Tuesday, predicting it would help sustain U.S. economic growth.
"I'm very optimistic about the ability of the American economy to stay strong," he told Reuters during a mission to promote small and medium-sized U.S. business in Canada.
"The foundation's there. I think this budget deal that was signed today, with our getting to a balanced budget in five years, is a tremendous asset to the business community, to our government.
"So I think all the pieces are in place. Consumer confidence is high. Our companies are extremely competitive and productive."
He said the U.S. economy was nonetheless unlikely to match the torrid first-quarter growth rate of almost five percent. It grew by 2.2 percent in the second quarter.
But he said the fact that the government had gotten control of its spending and taken many of the steps that businesses were required to take "gives the business community a lot of confidence."
On the down side for the economy is the strike against United Parcel Service (UPS).
"Obviously if it lasts for a long time, it will have a negative impact on the economy. As of right now, my reading is that the impact has not been great," he said.
He repeated the White House's unwillingness to take action on UPS under the Taft-Hartley Act, which allows a president to intervene in a strike if it endangers the nation's economy.

"At this point the president's not seen the circumstances which allow him to take advantage of the legal authority given to him," Daley said, noting, however, that Clinton had strongly encouraged the parties to get back to the table.
Regarding economic relations with Canada, Daley said he believed that the strength of growth in Canada's economy "will obviously help the opportunity for American companies to sell here."
The U.S. trade deficit with Canada widened in May, but he declined to predict its future course.
